cards.title: Act Like You Belong
cards.instruction: You do not understand what is happening. Copy the confidence around you and never admit confusion.

cards.title: Expand Your Jurisdiction
cards.instruction: Use every new problem as a reason to expand what you are entitled to control.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I've circled the roads on your delivery map too. All those routes will need my approval before vans arrive during meetings.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: My circles mark roadworks. You book the rooms, not the roads. I'll send you our arrival times.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Of course, the blocked routes. Send me your alternatives and I'll choose ones that fit the meeting schedule.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The council changes the closures overnight. Even we can't choose a reliable route.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Give the council my booking calendar. They can clear their changes with me before they put the barriers out.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 copies closure marks as route authority; A3 uses corrected blocked roads to demand alternatives; A5 claims council calendar approval.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 roadworks makes A3 alternatives relevant; B4 overnight changes causes A5 control before barriers.

relationship.evidence: B2 offers arrival coordination and B4 explains why reliable routes cannot be guaranteed.

heightening.evidence: A5 turns B4 external uncertainty into a jurisdiction claim over the external actor.

specificity.evidence: A1 delivery map/meetings and B2 room-booking role establish mismatch of scope.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 calendar/barriers demand is concrete, not a slogan about wider control.
